restatement.intent: Give every operation exactly one data record describing its name, receiver, arguments (type, unit, default, limits, docs), cross-argument rules, result shape, flags and implementation, and make every consumer read that record instead of keeping its own copy.
restatement.problem: When several consumers (checker, help, error messages, agent context, tests) each hold their own idea of what an operation accepts and returns, they drift, and callers — especially agents — get plausible-looking wrong behaviour instead of a precise refusal.
restatement.solution: Register one validated OpRecord per (receiver kind, name) into a registry. A binder looks up the record, matches arguments, fills defaults, checks types and limits in the declared unit, runs the cross-argument hook, and returns bound arguments plus warnings or a structured Failure. The diagnoser turns a Failure into a refusal built from the same record (valid names, nearest name, redirect, fix), the describer renders short and long help from it, and a walker test calls every record with its own sample arguments and checks the declared result fields.

quiz.answer: It binds successfully and carries a RANGE warning with the record's usualHint. Only a value outside the hard min/max is a refusal, and defaults never warn — only values the caller actually supplied.

The walker test (goja-cv's TestRegistryWalk / TestSchemaProperty). Missing samples are caught at registration, but registration can only require them if the samples live in the record rather than in the test file.
quiz.where: Structure (Walker); Collaborations 6; Implementation notes §5; 'the walker test' sketch

quiz.answer: Because method, help and look redirects sit in three tables outside the registry, so a redirect added to one table is invisible to the others — the diagnoser then gives inconsistent repairs for the same near-miss.
The binder (call checking, warnings) and the describer (context line and full help); the diagnoser and the walker are two more.

transfer.why: Three independent consumers (LLM tool descriptions, mobile control UI, hub validation) plus plug-in authors who add actions without reading the hub's source is exactly the stated applicability. It also forces the chapter's under-specified case — records arriving at run time from third parties — so the host-override rules matter more than in goja-cv.

participants.Operation record: One per (device kind, action name): set_temperature on Thermostat, dim_lights on Lamp, lock_door on Lock, run_scene on Scene.
participants.Argument spec: temperature (number, unit °C, min 5, max 30, usual [16,24], hint 'use set_mode for off'), brightness (number 0–100 %), duration (number, seconds), target (enum with valueDocs).
participants.Flags: class (climate, lighting, security, scene), confirm for lock_door and run_scene set by the hub (not the plug-in), internal for maintenance actions, identity/anonymous flags for idempotent reads.
participants.Registry: Hub-side registry keyed by device kind and action name; validates plug-in records and refuses name clashes between plug-ins.
participants.Binder: Hub command path, shared by voice-assistant commands and app commands so both get identical refusals.
participants.Describer: Two renderings: contextLine() = the tool description the LLM sees; controlSpec() = type, unit, limits and options the app draws one widget per argument.
participants.Diagnoser: Builds refusals for malformed commands from either consumer: valid actions, nearest action name, key redirects ('dim' → dim_lights, 'brightness' on a Thermostat).
participants.Walker: CI test that runs every registered action against a mock device per plug-in and compares result keys with declared fields.

transfer.sketch:
value OpRecord: name, on: DeviceKind, args: [ArgSpec], validate?(args) → ok | Failure,
                returns: Ack, fields(boundArgs) → [FieldSpec],
                flags: {class, confirm: none|session|user, internal}, redirects?, samples, doc, run | expand

-- plug-in load: per-record structural checks now, cross-record checks after the batch
registry.register(rec) → ok | refuse(E_BAD_RECORD, …)
registry.seal()   -- redirect targets exist, no name clash; re-run after every plug-in batch
-- the hub rewrites flags.confirm from its own policy table; a plug-in cannot lower it

hub.receive(cmd) → reply
  bound = bind(cmd.on, cmd.name, cmd.args)
  if bound is Failure: return explain(bound, registry)
  if policy(bound.rec).confirm == user and not cmd.confirmed:
      return refuse(E_NEEDS_CONFIRM, fix: same call with confirmed: true)  -- non-interactive: refuse
  return run(bound) ⊕ { warnings: bound.warnings }

describer.contextLine(rec)  -- ~1 line per callable action, for the LLM tool list
controlSpec(rec)            -- per-arg type/unit/limits/options, for the app's widget
walker: for rec in registry.all(): assert run(bind(rec.on, rec.name, rec.samples)) matches rec.fields
key_notes: §1 (validate structure and consistency): most important here. Third-party records arrive after start-up, so the chapter's 'check cross-record rules once at end of start-up' has to become 'after each plug-in batch'; otherwise a plug-in's redirect can dangle or collide and no call ever fails until an agent hits it.

§2 (hard limits vs usual ranges, in the declared unit): a voice assistant says °F or 'a bit warmer' while the app's slider is °C — units and limits must live in the ArgSpec, not in either consumer, or the two UIs disagree about what 22 means.
Flags / confirm row: the hub must own confirm per action and cap what a plug-in may declare; a plug-in that self-declares confirm: none on lock_door silently widens what the LLM is allowed to call.
§8 (defaults are part of identity): a plug-in bumping set_temperature's default must be treated as a behaviour change, or every saved scene and automation changes meaning silently on upgrade.
§4 (keep near-miss redirects in the records): 'dim' → dim_lights and brightness-on-a-thermostat must live in the same records the app and the LLM read, or the two get different repairs.
§9 (enumerate exceptions): hub-level things that are not device actions still need one visible list with a test that every reachable name is in the registry or that list.
transfer.risk: Letting plug-ins own their own flags and cross-record redirects: a third-party record then decides its own confirm policy, collides with another plug-in's action name, or redirects into a stranger's action, and the permissive record is what the LLM's tool description shows. Second risk: generating the mobile UI straight from ArgSpec yields sliders for enumerations and no grouping or layout, so the app looks machine-made.

transfer.why: The chapter's own Applicability rule excludes it: 'the platform already gives you the records (a typed RPC schema that generates clients, docs and validation); use that schema as the registry instead of building a parallel one.' A Go registry beside the .proto files recreates exactly the drift the pattern exists to remove — two descriptions of the same method, one of which will be stale.

participants.Operation record: The protobuf method plus its message and annotation constraints — already the record; a second Go record is the anti-pattern here.
participants.Argument spec: Field definitions with buf/validate or custom option annotations (min/max, required, enum values, docs).
participants.Flags: Custom method options only if they are genuinely missing (idempotency, confirmation); add them as annotations rather than in Go.
participants.Registry: The compiled file descriptor set, read at run time — a projection of the .proto, not a copy of it.
participants.Binder: The generated/annotated validator on the server plus the client-side check; one implementation, driven by descriptors.
participants.Describer: A renderer over descriptors (comment → doc line, annotations → limits), producing help and the agent's tool list.
participants.Diagnoser: Deserialises the structured refusal into help text; it reads the same descriptors for valid field names.
participants.Walker: Walks the descriptor set and calls each method against a test double, asserting response fields against declared ones.

key_notes: Applicability, 'do not use it when the platform already gives you the records' — this decision is settled there, not by how nice the Go table would look.

If a registry is still wanted, §1's lesson applies inverted: it must be derived from the descriptor set at start-up and refuse to start when it disagrees with a .proto, so it is never a second source of truth.

§2 and §4 (units, ranges, redirects) point at the real gap: plain protobuf has no 'usual range' or near-miss redirect, so those belong in annotations and in a diagnoser layer, not in a parallel record.
transfer.risk: Approving it 'just for help text' and ending up with two field lists: the validator honours the .proto, the help honours the Go table, and the first renamed or newly required field makes the help lie to agents — the documentation-drift failure the chapter opens with.

review_notes.note: Three different rules for the same check. The Solution says validate each record at registration 'for structure and for consistency (… redirects that exist)'; note 1 says cross-record checks run at the end of start-up, not record by record; note 4 says keep redirects in the records and that goja-cv keeps them outside, which is debt; note 8 says 'validate redirects at registration'. A reader cannot tell what to implement, and the transfer case of plug-ins registering later has no rule at all.
review_notes.suggestion: State one rule explicitly and use it everywhere: per-record structural checks in register(); cross-record checks (redirect targets, (on,name) uniqueness across modules) in a separate registry.seal() called once after all modules and again after each late or plug-in batch, with the reason given (a redirect may point at an operation another module registers later).

review_notes.note: Flags are the participant with the least specification and the most consequences. 'flags' has no type in the sketch, the flag names are only listed inside a table cell, the confirm flag appears nowhere in the sketch or the Collaborations, the host-cannot-be-lowered rule is one clause, and nothing says how the binder knows a run is non-interactive.
review_notes.suggestion: Add a short Flags subsection: the enumerated flags with type and default, who may set each (host policy vs record author), the precedence rule when a host and a record both set one, what registration does with an unknown flag name (refuse), and how interactive vs non-interactive is decided and passed to the binder.

review_notes.section: Applicability ('added at run time') vs Collaborations and note 1
review_notes.note: The pattern claims to serve operations 'added often, by several people, or by users at run time', but every validation story assumes a start-up that finishes ('a malformed record fails registration before any call', 'at the end of start-up'). Run-time registration has no ordering, no reseal, and no statement of what happens to already-bound calls or cached results when a record is replaced.
review_notes.suggestion: Add a note on late registration: batch multiple records into one seal, re-run cross-record checks after each batch, refuse replacement of a record that bound calls or cached graph nodes already reference unless the default and result shape are unchanged, and say how a newly registered name enters the agent's context mid-session.

review_notes.note: fix: clamp(value, spec) hands the caller a silently altered call, which contradicts the chapter's own strongest principle in note 3 (silent acceptance is the worst outcome, because the result looks plausible). Clamping a radius of 400 to 200 may preserve intent; clamping a temperature of 40 on a 5–30 limit to 30 does not.
review_notes.suggestion: Refuse with the limits and, at most, the nearest legal bound as an explicit suggestion the caller must acknowledge — not as a 'fix' field that a caller replays verbatim. Say in the note which clamps preserve intent and which do not.

review_notes.note: The short context is named as a deliverable ('a short form for the agent's standing context', the 8× ratio) but its selection rule is never given: which records get a line, in what order, whether internal or class flags filter it, and what gives way when the catalogue grows. This is the part a reader implementing the pattern must decide first.
review_notes.suggestion: State the rule: contextLine for every callable record, internal excluded, ordered by class then name, with a stated budget and what is dropped when the budget is exceeded (e.g. collapse a class to one line naming its operations).

review_notes.note: fields is declared as a function of the bound arguments, but the walker binds exactly one samples set per record, so any result shape that only one option produces is never checked. Note 5 admits 'one happy-path call per record does not exercise … optional arguments' but offers no mechanism to fix it.
review_notes.suggestion: Make samples a list of argument sets, one per result-shape branch, and have registration require every declared branch to be covered by at least one sample; the walker then compares keys per sample rather than once per record.

review_notes.note: Redirects cover erroneous keys and method names, but not erroneous values. An agent writing interpolation: "bicubic" where the record enumerates "cubic", or a colour name with a typo, gets a plain ARG_TYPE with the valid set and no nearest value — even though options and valueDocs already make the nearest value computable.
review_notes.suggestion: Add a value-level redirect: on an enumeration failure, include nearest(failure.value, spec.options) and, when a valueDoc names it, the doc line; same refusal kind, one more field.

review_notes.section: Motivation bullet 3 and Implementation note 3; Implementation note 6
review_notes.note: The cv.open encoding anecdote is told twice in near-identical wording, and note 6's 'goja-cv's binder is the largest file in its graph package' is a build fact that does not help a reader apply the pattern. Note 9's Editor-lab counterexample is likewise a third telling of the same drift story.
review_notes.suggestion: Tell the encoding failure once, in Motivation, and in note 3 only draw the rule. Replace file-size claims with the design consequence. Keep the Editor lab only as a one-line 'known cost' pointer, or cut it.

review_notes.section: Structure (Operation record / Registry) and method-level redirects
review_notes.note: The Structure table says method-level redirects live 'in the operation record or the registry', the sketch puts redirects? on OpRecord, and the diagnoser calls registry.redirectFor — the reader cannot tell which is authoritative, or what wins if both define a redirect for the same name.
review_notes.suggestion: Pick one home (the record) and let the registry hold only the derived index it builds at seal time; state the conflict rule, e.g. a record-level redirect beats a registry-level one and registration refuses duplicates.

ratings.comment: The participant model, the do-not-use list and the non-image examples make the pattern genuinely transferable, but the redirect-validation rules contradict each other across three places, flags are left untyped and undescribed, and the run-time-registration case the pattern advertises has no validation story — so a reader would have to redesign those parts before applying it.
